newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans increasingly call for death penalty -- poll. [corrected 11:55 gmt]
newsitem.headline: S.Africans increasingly call for death penalty -- poll. [corrected 11:55 gmt]

text.p: South Africans hardened by spiralling crime are increasingly demanding the return of state hangings for violent criminals, with a new poll showing 80 percent of urban residents want the death penalty reinstated.

Research Surveys (corrects name from Market Research Africa) said on Tuesday the poll reflected a marked increase in support for the death penalty from two years ago when 80 percent of whites but only 49 percent of blacks were in favour of hangings.
South Africa's Constitutional Court abolished the death penalty in June 1995, lifting the threat of hanging from 453 prisoners on death row.
While political violence has slumped since President Nelson Mandela came to power at the head of a unity government in 1994, crime, including rape, murder and car hijacks, has soared.
A huge increase was shown among blacks this year, with 76 percent of those surveyed calling for the death penalty compared to 94 percent of whites, the researchers said in a statement.

In 1995, half the black women polled were in favour of the death penalty. It jumped to 84 percent this year. White women followed the same trend: in 1995 76 percent were in favour, rising to 95 percent this year.

Black men also showed a hardening attitude to violent criminals, calls for the death penality increasing from 48 percent in 1995 to 68 percent this year. White men showed a lesser increase from 86 percent two years ago to 93 percent this year.
Rising crime in South Africa, particularly in the Gauteng region centred on Johannesburg, is scaring off investment and foreign tourists and is one of the main causes of an exodus of skilled people.

Vigilante action is also on the increase: in the latest incident a man suspected of raping a 34-year-old woman at the weekend was severely beaten by township residents before police arrested him. He is in a critical condition in hospital.
